title: Emory's 2026 Sheth Lecture Takes On the Indian Constitution, October 15 in Atlanta
excerpt: Emory law professor Deepa Das Acevedo delivers "Dynamic Equilibrium in the Indian Constitution" at Tull Auditorium at 4:30 p.m. Thursday — free and open to the public.
body:
• Emory University's 2026 Sheth Lecture in India Studies, titled "Dynamic Equilibrium in the Indian Constitution," will be delivered by Dr. Deepa Das Acevedo, Associate Professor of Law at Emory University School of Law.
  • The lecture is on Thursday, October 15 at 4:30 p.m. at Tull Auditorium, Emory School of Law, Atlanta — and it is open to the public.
  • Visitors can park free of charge after 4 p.m. in the Gambrell Parking Deck behind the law school; the article announcing the lecture lists no registration or ticket requirement.
  • The Sheth Lecture is an endowed annual series funded by a gift from Dr. Jagdish N. Sheth and Madhuri Sheth, and this year's edition is hosted by Emory's Center for the Study of Law and Religion.

Atlanta's Indian diaspora has a date with constitutional law this week. Emory University's 2026 Sheth Lecture in India Studies — titled "Dynamic Equilibrium in the Indian Constitution" — will be delivered on Thursday, October 15 at 4:30 p.m. by Dr. Deepa Das Acevedo, Associate Professor of Law at Emory University School of Law, NRI Pulse reported. The lecture takes place at Tull Auditorium at the Emory School of Law and is open to the public.

The Lecture and the Lecturer

Das Acevedo's subject is the idea of dynamic equilibrium in India's constitutional framework — the notion that the Constitution holds competing forces, including Parliament, the courts, the states and fundamental rights, in a balance that shifts over time without breaking. It is a live question in Indian public life: the running arguments in New Delhi over judicial appointments, federal power and the basic structure doctrine are, at bottom, arguments about exactly that equilibrium. A lecture that names the mechanism gives diaspora audiences — many of whom follow Indian constitutional fights closely during election and court seasons — a framework rather than another headline.

The event is hosted and organised by Emory's Center for the Study of Law and Religion, a fitting home for a talk that sits at the junction of law, institutions and public life.

A Series Built by the Diaspora

The Sheth Lecture in India Studies is an annual, endowed series made possible by a gift from Dr. Jagdish N. Sheth and Madhuri Sheth, among Emory's most prominent Indian American benefactors. Jagdish Sheth, the Charles H. Kellstadt Professor of Marketing at Emory's Goizueta Business School, and his wife have supported Indian studies at the university for decades; the lecture series brings distinguished scholars to Atlanta to present interdisciplinary research to the academic community and the broader public. Past editions of the Sheth Lecture in Indian Studies have featured speakers including author Salman Rushdie, filmmaker Deepa Mehta and activist Medha Patkar, according to Emory News.

Going? The Practical Details

The lecture begins at 4:30 p.m. on Thursday, October 15 at Tull Auditorium, Emory University School of Law, Atlanta. It is open to the public, and the announcement lists no registration, ticket or RSVP requirement. Visitors can park free of charge after 4 p.m. in the Gambrell Parking Deck, located behind the School of Law — arrive a little early, as public lectures in the series draw from both the university and Atlanta's Indian community.

Why It Matters

Endowed lectures like this one are part of the institutional backbone of diaspora intellectual life: they put Indian constitutional scholarship on an American university stage, in a city whose Indian community is one of the fastest-growing in the South. For students weighing law, public policy or South Asian studies, it is also a rare chance to hear a specialist work through India's constitutional design in person — and to ask questions afterwards.
